Umbrella review, November 2026

Evidence review

A systematic review of 345 published meta-analyses and key studies across the seven areas this program covers, with 454 pooled results compared side by side.

At a glance

What the published evidence says, taken together

In shortWe ran a systematic search for published meta-analyses in the seven areas this program covers and compared their results side by side. Three patterns run through all of them: effects depend on who measures them, they shrink when checked harder, and the everyday strategies people rely on most are the least tested.

304database searches, logged
4,086titles screened
345reviews and key studies included
454pooled results extracted
100%of numbers confirmed against the source
87topics with no pooled answer

Seven findings

  1. Who rates the outcome decides the result. Non-drug treatments for children keep about 50% of their effect when the rater doesn't know who was treated. Medication keeps 96%. See the chart.
  2. Effects shrink under scrutiny. Across 12 before-and-after pairs, the later or better-controlled estimate kept a median of 37% of the first. See the chart.
  3. Inconsistency is the signal, not average performance. People with ADHD respond at normal speed most of the time. What differs is the occasional very slow response. See the chart.
  4. Tests and ratings measure different things. They barely correlate, and treatments that move one often don't move the other. See the chart.
  5. Little of this is specific to ADHD. The same differences appear at similar sizes in depression, autism, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia. See the chart.
  6. The most popular catalysts are the least tested. 8 of the 11 engagement signals have never been pooled in people with ADHD. Deadlines and timers have no pooled evidence in anyone, and body doubling rests on one 12-person study. See the table.
  7. AI results weaken as checks tighten, and adding a human doesn't automatically help. See the numbers.

This is an umbrella review: a review of published reviews. It compares pooled results that other teams calculated. It did not re-analyse individual trials, it was not registered in advance with a registry, and the searching and extraction were done by AI research assistants, one per area, with every number then checked against its source. Read the cross-area patterns as leads to test, not as settled results. Nothing here is medical advice.

The review plan

How the review was done

In shortThe question, sources, inclusion rules and comparisons were written down before any searching. Every extracted number was then checked against the paper it came from.

Question

Across the seven areas this program covers, what do published meta-analyses say about the size, consistency and certainty of effects? And what patterns appear only when the areas are compared with each other?

Design

An umbrella review (a systematic review of meta-analyses), followed by a comparison of the pooled results across areas. Protocol fixed on 18 November 2026, before searching.

Sources

Europe PMC, which includes PubMed and preprints, searched through its public interface with every query and hit count logged. Named reviews outside it (psychology and economics journals, Cochrane) were located by web search and recorded separately.

What was included

Meta-analyses, network meta-analyses and large consortium analyses from 2015 to November 2026, in people, reporting a pooled estimate. Where a topic had none, the largest single study was recorded and the topic flagged as a gap.

From search to data

  1. 304 searches run
  2. 6,898 records returned
  3. 4,086 titles screened
  4. 345 sources included
  5. 541 results recorded
  6. 454 numbers confirmed

Records returned are not de-duplicated between searches, so the same paper can be counted more than once. Of the 541 results, 454 carry a number and 87 record a gap or a review that gave no pooled figure.

How the numbers were checked

A script fetched the abstract for every source and looked for each extracted effect size and confidence interval in it. That confirmed 412 numbers. Numbers read from full text, preprints or sources outside PubMed went to a separate manual check against the original; 42 were confirmed that way. All numbers used on this page were confirmed. No included source is marked as retracted, and every author and year matched the database record.

Comparisons planned in advance

  1. Rater: blinded against unblinded ratings of the same treatment.
  2. Time: whether pooled effects shrink in later reviews.
  3. Precision: whether small bodies of evidence report larger effects.
  4. Level against variability: average performance compared with within-person inconsistency.
  5. Age: children compared with adults.
  6. Evidence against use: how well-tested an approach is, compared with how widely it is recommended.
  7. Catalyst signal: effects grouped by the engagement signal they deliver.

Two further comparisons emerged from the data and are labelled exploratory: tests against ratings, and ADHD against other diagnoses.

Limits of this review
  • It works from review-level results. Trials were not re-extracted, so errors in the original reviews carry through.
  • Reviews of the same topic share many of the same trials. The results are therefore not independent, and the cross-area statistics are descriptive.
  • Searching and extraction were done by AI research assistants, one per area, without a second independent extractor. English only, one database family.
  • Effect sizes on different scales were converted to a common scale for the overview only. Accuracy figures and prevalences were kept separate.
  • Paired comparisons sometimes come from different reviews with different inclusion rules. Each pair names its sources so you can judge.
  • The protocol was not lodged with a public registry.

Findings

The typical pooled effect is modest everywhere

In shortIn every one of the seven areas the middle pooled effect falls between 0.30 and 0.49. Individual headline results that look much bigger than this deserve a second look.

Effect sizes here are standardized differences. As a rough guide, 0.2 is small, 0.5 is medium and 0.8 is large. The chart shows the median of 320 confirmed pooled results that could be put on that scale.

Finding 1

Who rates the outcome decides the result

In shortWhen the person rating symptoms knows who got the treatment, non-drug treatments look about twice as effective. Medication in children is the exception: it holds up whoever rates it.

50% kept

Non-drug treatments in children, median of 6 pairs (range 11% to 64%).

96% kept

Medication in children, parent against teacher ratings, 3 pairs.

70% kept

Medication in adults, self-rating against clinician rating, 4 pairs. Here the person taking the medicine is the more cautious judge.

The comparison group matters as much as the rater. In one Cochrane review, cognitive behavioural therapy for adults improved self-rated symptoms by 0.84 against a waiting list and by 0.16 against supportive therapy.

What this means for the program: every study should report a blinded or objective outcome alongside self-report, and compare against an active control, not a waiting list.

Finding 2

Effects shrink under scrutiny

In shortWhen more trials arrive, samples grow, publication bias is corrected, or the intervention ends, most effects lose more than half their size. The one clear exception is methylphenidate in children, unchanged over ten years of Cochrane reviews.

37% kept

Median across all 12 pairs.

9 of 12

pairs lost more than half of the original effect.

ρ = -0.24

Across 183 pooled treatment effects, newer reviews report smaller effects (p = 0.0013; exploratory, results are not independent).

What this means for the program: plan pilots on the assumption that a published effect will come in at about a third of its size, pre-register outcomes, and measure again after the intervention stops.

Finding 3

Inconsistency is the signal, not average performance

In shortOn reaction-time tasks, people with ADHD are as fast as anyone on a typical response. The difference is in the occasional very slow one. Measures of inconsistency beat measures of average level every time both were pooled.

There are two cautions. Inconsistency separates ADHD from healthy controls well (0.76 in children) but hardly from other clinical groups (0.25). And the difference fades with age, from 0.76 in children to 0.46 in adults.

What this means for the program: this supports measuring each person against themselves across tasks and days, as the Interest Gradient and Starting Delay measures do, in preference to a single average score. It also means those measures need testing against other clinical groups, not just healthy volunteers.

Finding 4 · exploratory

Tests and ratings measure different things

In shortQuestionnaires show an executive-function gap three times larger than tests do, and the two barely agree. Medication moves ratings more than tests. Brain training does the reverse.

0.54 against 1.76

Executive function in children with ADHD compared with other children: on tests, then on rating questionnaires, in the same review.

r = 0.19

Typical correlation between an executive-function test and a rating of the same skill.

r = 0.14

Correlation between how people rate their own thinking and how they score, across conditions and 92,606 people.

Yet in health registers, time on medication goes with fewer serious events: all-cause mortality 25% lower, suicidal behaviour 17% lower, substance misuse 15% lower, criminality 13% lower, transport accidents 12% lower, injuries 24% lower. These are observational comparisons, mostly of the same people on and off medication, so they show association and not proof.

What this means for the program: neither a rating scale nor a lab task is enough alone. The profile needs a third anchor in daily life, such as whether and when real tasks get started.

Finding 5 · exploratory

Little of this is specific to ADHD

In shortPreferring a smaller reward now over a larger one later is as strong in depression and schizophrenia as in ADHD, and stronger in bipolar disorder. Differences shrink by half or more when ADHD is compared with other clinical groups in place of healthy volunteers.

Executive-function tests show the same gap in autism (0.48) as in ADHD (0.45), and the genetic overlap between ADHD and every other symptom family is about 0.5 at every age.

What this means for the program: this is the strongest support in the review for the cross-diagnosis profile. It also sets a rule for study design: recruit clinical comparison groups from the start.

Finding 6

The most popular catalysts are the least tested

In shortBefore correction, almost every engagement strategy shows an effect of about 0.3 to 0.5, whatever signal it delivers. After correction or follow-up, what remains is 0.04 to 0.20. Deadlines, timers, body doubling and treat bundling have no pooled evidence at all.

Someone else's signal works better

Incentives set by someone else: about 0.5. Rewards people give themselves: 0.17.

Packages beat ingredients

Peer support inside a full programme: 0.34. The peer-support part tested alone: 0.08.

Only 8% lasted

Of 54 exercise-prompting programmes tested head to head on 61,293 people, 8% still showed an effect after the four weeks ended.

Two things stand out for this program. White or pink noise is the one clear case where the same catalyst helps one group (+0.25 with ADHD) and hurts another (−0.21 without). And no study anywhere has tested rotating catalysts as they wear off, which is what the program proposes.

What this means for the program: the first catalyst trials should be the untested ones people already use (body doubling, external deadlines, treat bundling) and a direct test of rotation. The 2002 study usually cited for externally set deadlines was retracted in 2026 and failed replication, so the program should not lean on it.

Finding 7

AI results weaken as checks tighten

In shortAI models look accurate on small samples and their own data, and much less so on large samples and other people's data. Simulated participants get the direction of an effect right but overstate its size. A person plus an AI is often worse than the better of the two alone.

Accuracy falls with sample size

Classifying depression from brain scans: up to 95% accurate with 20 people, 61% with 1,868, in the same data. Between 83% and 94.5% of psychiatric prediction models are rated at high risk of bias.

Models don't travel

Treatment-response models score about 0.80 to 0.85 on their own data. In the reference test across independent schizophrenia trials, a model built on some trials did no better than chance on the next.

Simulated participants overstate effects

Language models reproduced 73% to 81% of published main effects but only 46% to 63% of interactions. Their effects were two to three times larger than in people, and they "found" an effect in 68% to 83% of cases where the human study found none.

Human plus AI is not automatically better

Across 106 experiments, human-AI teams did worse than the better of the two alone (−0.23), and worse still on decision tasks (−0.27). Language models alone identified a condition in 94.9% of cases; lay users working with the same models did so in under 34.5%.

AI-discovered drugs

Phase I success is high, about 80%. Phase II success was put at about 40% in 2024 and 19.5% in a 2026 analysis of 129 candidates, close to the usual industry rate.

Chatbots and apps

Mental-health chatbots and apps improve depressive symptoms by about 0.3 on self-report, with roughly one in five users dropping out. Digital ADHD treatments show 0.33 overall and 0.12 with blinded raters.

What this means for the program: the AI engine should treat simulated effects as two to three times too large until calibrated, count simulated "positives" as weak evidence, and require a test on outside data at each gate. Human sign-off alone is not a safeguard: the gates need independent checks, not just a person approving what the model suggests.

Also found

What fades with age and what doesn't

In shortMedication effects and task-based markers are smaller in adults than in children. Restlessness measured by motion sensors stays the same, and difficulty regulating emotion is larger.

What this means for the program: an adult profile should give weight to movement and emotion regulation, where the adult signal is strongest, and should not assume that markers validated in children carry over.

Gaps

Where there is no pooled evidence

In shortA gap here means the search found no meta-analysis, or only a single study. These are the places where a small, careful study would add the most.

Several gaps sit at the centre of this program: rejection sensitivity, hyperfocus and interest-based attention, effort cost, task initiation, the aperiodic EEG slope, blink rate and pupil measures, hormonal effects in women, body doubling, and any test of matching or rotating strategies to the person.

So what

What this changes in the research plan

  1. Three kinds of outcome in every study: a blinded or objective measure, a self-report, and a daily-life measure such as real tasks started.
  2. Active controls and clinical comparison groups from the first pilot, since waiting lists and healthy volunteers both inflate results.
  3. Assume a third. Size pilots on one third of the published effect, pre-register, and measure again after the intervention ends.
  4. Measure inconsistency within the person, not average level, and check it against other diagnoses.
  5. Test the untested catalysts first: body doubling, external deadlines, treat bundling and rotation, each against an active control.
  6. Calibrate the AI engine before trusting it: shrink simulated effects, require outside-data tests at every gate, and give human reviewers independent evidence, not just the model's recommendation.
  7. Fill the central gaps with small, well-measured studies: rejection sensitivity, hyperfocus, effort cost, and task initiation.

These are proposals drawn from published evidence for research planning. They are not treatment advice, and no one should start, stop or change a medicine or supplement because of this page.
